title: ImageNet
text:
The ILSVRC aims to "follow in the footsteps" of the smaller-scale PASCAL VOC challenge, established in 2005, which contained only about 20,000 images and twenty object classes.[1] To "democratize" ImageNet, Fei-Fei Li proposed to the PASCAL VOC team a collaboration, beginning in 2010, where research teams would evaluate their algorithms on the given data set, and compete to achieve higher accuracy on several visual recognition tasks.[2]

The resulting annual competition is now known as the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC). The ILSVRC uses a "trimmed" list of only 1000 image categories or "classes", including 90 of the 120 dog breeds classified by the full ImageNet schema.[1]

The 2010s saw dramatic progress in image processing.

The first competition in 2010 had 11 participating teams. The winning team was a linear support vector machine (SVM). The features are a dense grid of HoG and LBP, sparsified by local coordinate coding and pooling.[3] It achieved 52.9% in classification accuracy and 71.8% in top-5 accuracy. It was trained for 4 days on three 8-core machines (dual quad-core 2 GHz Intel Xeon CPU).[4]

The second competition in 2011 had fewer teams, with another SVM winning at top-5 error rate 25%.[5] The winning team was XRCE by Florent Perronnin, Jorge Sanchez. The system was another linear SVM, running on quantized[6] Fisher vectors.[7,8] It achieved 74.2% in top-5 accuracy.

In 2012, a deep convolutional neural net called AlexNet achieved 84.7% in top-5 accuracy, a great leap forward.[9] The second place was by Oxford VGG, which uses the previous generic architecture of SVM, SIFT, color statistics, Fisher vectors, etc.[10] In the next couple of years, top-5 accuracy grew to above 90%. While the 2012 breakthrough "combined pieces that were all there before", the dramatic quantitative improvement marked the start of an industry-wide artificial intelligence boom.[11]

In 2013, most high-ranking entries used convolutional neural networks. The winning entry for object localization was the OverFeat, an architecture for simultaneous object classification and localization.[12] The winning entry for classification was an ensemble of multiple CNNs by Clarifai.[1]

By 2014, more than 50 institutions participated in the ILSVRC.[1] The winning entry for classification was GoogLeNet.[13] The winning entry for localization was VGGNet. In 2017, 29 of 38 competing teams had greater than 95% accuracy.[14] In 2017 ImageNet stated it would roll out a new, much more difficult challenge in 2018 that involves classifying 3D objects using natural language. Because creating 3D data is more costly than annotating a pre-existing 2D image, the dataset is expected to be smaller. The applications of progress in this area would range from robotic navigation to augmented reality.[15]

In 2015, the winning entry was ResNet, which exceeded human performance.[16,17] However, as one of the challenge's organizers, Olga Russakovsky, pointed out in 2015, the ILSVRC is over only 1000 categories; humans can recognize a larger number of categories, and also (unlike the programs) can judge the context of an image.[18]

In 2016, the winning entry was CUImage, an ensemble model of 6 networks: Inception v3, Inception v4, Inception ResNet v2, ResNet 200, Wide ResNet 68, and Wide ResNet 3.[19] The runner-up was ResNeXt, which combines the Inception module with ResNet.[20]

In 2017, the winning entry was the Squeeze-and-Excitation Network (SENet), reducing the top-5 error to 2.251%.[21]

The organizers of the competition stated in 2017 that the 2017 competition would be the last one, since the benchmark has been solved and no longer posed a challenge. They also stated that they would organize a new competition on 3D images.[15] However, such a competition never materialized.
